newsitem.title: FRANCE: French transport unions split over bosses' offer.
newsitem.headline: French transport unions split over bosses' offer.

text.p: Striking French bus and train drivers voted to extend a nine-day stoppage on Friday despite a split among unions over an employers' proposal to cut the working week.
In four hours of talks with unions, employers proposed cutting the working week for bus, tram and Metro train drivers in provincial cities to 36.5 hours from 39 in exchange for greater state aid.

Leaders of the Communist-led CGT and the Socialist-led CFDT urged their members to extend the strike, hitting about 10 cities on Friday. But the independent Force Ouvriere said it wanted a suspension until a new round of talks next Friday.

On the ground, drivers in cities including Toulouse, Toulon, Cannes, Nice and Lille decided to extend the strike, judging the concessions inadequate. Unions want a 35-hour week and retirement at 55 rather than 60.
In Perpignan, however, transport was due to resume on Saturday. Other cities were due to decide on an extension later.
In the south-western city of Toulouse, drivers have been on strike for 19 days over the demands, which unions say would help combat record unemployment.

A CGT spokesman said "We told our comrades to continue to fight in the networks to get agreement on 35 hours. We must also demand the quick opening of real negotiations." The CFDT said the conflict might widen via a national strike.

FO Transport leader Roger Poletti said: "It seems that the employers have finally taken the measure of what's at stake in the conflict. They're starting to talk about early retirement and cutting working time over 18 months."
The FO said the government had guaranteed the UTP employers' group 1.14 billion francs ($200 million) in state aid over four years to help it cut working hours.
The stoppages, which began with a one-day protest in about 20 cities last Thursday, have spared Paris where drivers are already entitled to retire at 55.
The centre-right government bowed to truckers' demands for retirement at 55 after they blocked roads late last year.
It opposes extending the concession, saying it could bankrupt the pension system when post-war baby boomers start swelling the ranks of pensioners from 2005.
